title: Predicting Metacritic Scores from Steam Data
text: The GitHub repository containing all code used in this analysis can be found at https://github.com/rrtullis/sample-analysis.

title: Predicting Metacritic Scores from Steam Data
text:
Dataset
The data used in this analysis was sourced from Kaggle. It contains information fetched from Steam’s API and supplemental information from SteamSpy. Steam is a major platform for PC gaming, and holds ~70% market share. A full overview of the games dataset, with information on its features, can be found on the Data Documentation page under Additional Info.
The goal for this analysis was to predict the Metacritic score of a game. Metacritic is an American website that rates TV shows, movies, and video games on a scale of 0-100. The true score is calculated as a weighted average of ratings from top professional critic reviews. The distribution of Metacritic scores in this dataset is shown below.









The scores present in this dataset range from 6 to 97, with a mean of ~73.9 and a standard deviation of ~10.3. The distribution is somewhat left-skewed, but I opted not to transform metacritic_score, as I wanted my model’s predictions to be interpretable as the actual predicted score, rather than a transformation of the score.

title: Predicting Metacritic Scores from Steam Data
text:
Data Cleaning
The data used in this analysis was loaded from a .json and required extensive cleaning before it could be used. This cleaning involved manually typing each feature appropriately, dealing with placeholder missing values, and dropping any columns that wouldn’t be useful for analysis. A full walkthrough of this process can be found on the Data Cleaning page.
The main event for data cleaning came when dealing with five columns in particular: supported_languages, full_audio_languages, genres, and categories all contained lists of strings, and tags contained dictionaries. In order to convert these columns to a usuable format for analysis, I used sklearn’s MultiLabelBinarizer to convert the list columns to a set of binary columns, where a 1 in a given column (e.g., supported_languages_English) would indicate that, for instance, the game supports the English language.

games_encoded = games_typed.copy()
for f in list_features:
    mlb = MultiLabelBinarizer()
    transformed = mlb.fit_transform(games_typed[f]) # generate binary columns
    # convert to DataFrame & apply prefixes
    transformed_df = pd.DataFrame(transformed, columns=[f + "_" + str(c) for c in mlb.classes_], index=games_typed.index)
    games_encoded = pd.concat([games_encoded, transformed_df], axis=1)
    # drop original column
    games_encoded = games_encoded.drop(columns=[f])

As for tags, I used pandas’ json_normalize method to achieve a similar result, with the main difference that the added columns and values corresponded to key-value pairs in the dictionary. The final dataset that I used to train my models on had 4256 rows and 757 columns.

title: Predicting Metacritic Scores from Steam Data
text:
Iteration
Based off of the initial models’ performance, I chose to iterate on both ensemble tree models. I began with some modest tuning, which slightly improved their performance. As before, a full explanation of my process, along with the code required to reproduce my results, can be found on the Modeling page.
While modeling, I was concerned about the high dimensionality of my data, and thought that if I could distill my 756 features into a smaller number of columns I may get better results. My first attempt at this was to simply remove the columns generated from MultiLabelBinarizer and json_normalize from my training data. The resulting metrics were immediately poorer, and I opted to pursue another angle.
My next attempt involved using sklearn’s TruncatedSVD to generate new features that captured the variance of supported_languages, full_audio_languages, genres, categories, and tags. I used TruncatedSVD over standard PCA since, unlike PCA, TruncatedSVD does not center the data, making it better for sparse data like my own. I also opted to apply TruncatedSVD to each of the five groups of columns seperately because I wanted to preserve the domain of each group. When selecting how many features to return for each group, I made sure that I had enough to capture at least 90% of the variance in the category.
Unfortunately, even after tuning these models still performed worse than my modestly tuned models. What ultimately became my best-performing model was a XGBoost Regressor operating on the original dataset that had been subjected to extensive tuning. The only change was an added feature - the ratio of positive to negative votes, stored in positive_negative_ratio.

title: Predicting Metacritic Scores from Steam Data
text:
Final Model
The full preprocessing pipeline for my final model, along with its tuning grid, is shown below.

New Feature

games=games.copy()
games["positive_negative_ratio"] = games["positive"]/(games["negative"]+1)
num_features += ["positive_negative_ratio"]
features += ["positive_negative_ratio"]

# reinitialize the sets with the new feature
games_train, games_test = train_test_split(
    games,
    test_size=0.2,
    random_state=4025
)



Preprocessing Pipeline

dt_ord_prep = Pipeline([ # ordinal feature processing
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("ordinal_encoder", OrdinalEncoder())
])

dt_nom_prep = Pipeline([ # nominal feature processing
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("onehot_encoder", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="if_binary")),
    ("variance_threshold", VarianceThreshold(threshold=0.01))
])

dt_num_prep = Pipeline([ # numeric feature processing
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"))
])

dt_prep = ColumnTransformer([ # full preprocessing setup
    ("ord", dt_ord_prep, ord_features),
    ("nom", dt_nom_prep, nom_features),
    ("num", dt_num_prep, num_features)
])



Model & Tuning

xgb_pipe = Pipeline([ # xgb modeling pipeline
    ("preprocessor", dt_prep),
    ("model", XGBRegressor())
])

new_xgb_param_grid = { # new, expanded parameter grid
    "model__n_estimators": np.linspace(300, 1500, 20, dtype=int),
    "model__max_depth": [3, 4, 5, 6, 8],
    "model__learning_rate": np.logspace(-2.5, -0.5, 10),

    # 'randomness' parameters
    "model__subsample": np.linspace(0.6, 1.0, 5), # proportion of observations available to each tree
    "model__colsample_bytree": np.linspace(0.3, 1.0, 8), # proportion of columns available to each tree

    # split allowance parameters
    "model__min_child_weight": [1, 3, 5, 10], # minimum number of samples required in a leaf
    "model__gamma": [0, 0.1, 0.3, 1], # minimum reduction in loss required to split

    # regularization parameters
    "model__reg_alpha": np.logspace(-3, 1, 10), # encourages sparsity in leaves
    "model__reg_lambda": np.logspace(-2, 2, 10), # shrinks leaf weights 
}

new_xgb_rs = RandomizedSearchCV( 
    xgb_pipe,
    new_xgb_param_grid,
    n_iter=200,
    cv=rkf,
    scoring=["neg_mean_squared_error", "r2"],
    refit="neg_mean_squared_error",
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=4025
)

This tuning process found that the following parameters were optimal:

best_parameters = {
    "model__n_estimators": 1247,
    "model__max_depth": 6,
    "model__learning_rate": 0.000779,

    # 'randomness' parameters
    "model__subsample": 0.7, # proportion of observations available to each tree
    "model__colsample_bytree": 0.000999, # proportion of columns available to each tree

    # split allowance parameters
    "model__min_child_weight": 1, # minimum number of samples required in a leaf
    "model__gamma": 0.1, # minimum reduction in loss required to split

    # regularization parameters
    "model__reg_alpha": 0.000434, # encourages sparsity in leaves
    "model__reg_lambda": 4.6415, # shrinks leaf weights 
}

The final results of this model on the test set are shown below.

best_xgb = pickle.load(open("saved_objects/tuned_xgb.pkl", "rb"))
xgb_preds = best_xgb.predict(games_test[features])
xgb_r2 = r2_score(games_test[target], xgb_preds)
xgb_rmse = root_mean_squared_error(games_test[target], xgb_preds)
print("New XGBoost R2:", xgb_r2)
print("New XGBoost RMSE:", xgb_rmse)

New XGBoost R2: 0.5185717254641573
New XGBoost RMSE: 7.127757438729044


In the end, I had a tuned XGBoost Regressor that had a test RMSE of ~7.1 and an R2 score of ~0.52. I used permutation importance to determine which features the model relied on the most.

title: Predicting Metacritic Scores from Steam Data
text:
Interpretation
Based on my metrics, my model was able to explain ~52% of the variance in Metarcitic score, and made predictions that were, on average, off by ~7.1 points. This is a notable improvement over a dummy regressor, but is not particularly impressive overall. One reason for this mediocore performance may be that the games dataset does not contain information that is particularly relevant to a game’s Metacritic score. Most of the data used in this analysis was scraped from the Steam store, and while a storefront is a decent place to start collecting information, a game’s store presentation does not necessarily reflect how people will percieve or rate it. Were the dataset to contain more relevant information, I expect the performance metrics could be improved drastically.
As for the columns we do have, the model relies most heavily upon the engineered ratio of positive to negative votes, followed distantly by release date and the number of recommendations. Any future iterations of this project should focus more heavily on feature engineering that captures information related to how a game may be percieved by critics and players.

General Preprocessing
Though the data was cleaned in previous steps, there remains some general preprocessing that must be done when loading the data from games_clean.csv.

# load data
games = pd.read_csv("data/games_clean.csv")
games = games.drop(columns=["Unnamed: 0"]) # drop index column created by pandas when saving to csv

# fix typings
# convert datetime to unix timestamp
games["release_date"] = pd.to_datetime(games["release_date"], errors="coerce")
games["release_date"] = games["release_date"].astype("int64") // 10**9 # convert from nanoseconds to seconds
games["release_date"] = games["release_date"].astype("float64")

# convert estimated_owners to ordered category
games["estimated_owners"] = pd.Categorical(games["estimated_owners"],
                                           categories=["0 - 0",
                                                  "0 - 20000",
                                                  "20000 - 50000",
                                                  "50000 - 100000",
                                                  "100000 - 200000",
                                                  "200000 - 500000",
                                                  "500000 - 1000000",
                                                  "1000000 - 2000000",
                                                  "2000000 - 5000000",
                                                  "5000000 - 10000000",
                                                  "10000000 - 20000000",
                                                  "20000000 - 50000000",
                                                  "50000000 - 100000000",
                                                  "100000000 - 200000000"
                                                ], 
                                           ordered=True)                                     

The next step was genrating my general feature lists for use in numeric or categorical-specific pipelines. Previously, I intentionally stored all binary nominal features as integers to make this easier.

ord_features = ["estimated_owners"]
nom_features = games.select_dtypes(include=["int32", "int64"]).drop(columns=["release_date_month", 
                                                                             "release_date_year"]).columns.tolist()
cat_features = ord_features + nom_features

date_features = ["release_date_year", "release_date_month"]
num_features = games.select_dtypes(include=["float64"]).drop(columns=["metacritic_score"]).columns.tolist() + date_features

features = cat_features + num_features
target = "metacritic_score"

Lastly, I split the games into training and test sets, and set up a RepeatedKFold object for upcoming cross validation.

games_train, games_test = train_test_split(
    games,
    test_size=0.2,
    random_state=4025
)

rkf = RepeatedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=3, random_state=4025)



Dummy Regressor
As a baseline, I created a dummy regressor to compare potential models to. Its performance, along with that of all other models, can be seen in the table at the top of this page.

base = DummyRegressor(strategy="mean")
base.fit(games_train[features], games_train[target])
base_preds = base.predict(games_test[features])
base_r2 = r2_score(games_test[target], base_preds)
base_rmse = root_mean_squared_error(games_test[target], base_preds)



Linear Models
All linear models used the same preprocessing pipeline, shown below:

    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("ordinal_encoder", OrdinalEncoder())
])

lr_nom_prep = Pipeline([
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("onehot_encoder", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="if_binary")),
    ("variance_threshold", VarianceThreshold(threshold=0.01))
])

lr_num_prep = Pipeline([
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
    ("scaler", StandardScaler())
])

lr_prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("ord", lr_ord_prep, ord_features),
    ("nom", lr_nom_prep, nom_features),
    ("num", lr_num_prep, num_features)
])


Lasso
Lasso cross-validation is shown below:

lasso_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("preprocessor", lr_prep),
    ("model", Lasso())
])

lasso_cv_results = cross_validate(
    lasso_pipe,
    games_train[features],
    games_train[target],
    cv=rkf,
    scoring=["neg_mean_squared_error", "r2"]

title: Data Cleaning
text:
This page contains an overview of the data cleaning process for this sample analysis. Further information regarding the dataset can be found on the Data Documentation page under Additional Info.
For this analysis, my goal was to predict the Metacritic score of a game based on the features included in this dataset. A Metacritic score is a 0-100 rating of a video game’s overall quality, and is generated by Metacritic by gathering and taking a weighted average of reviews from top critics and publications.

Loading Data
Data was loaded from a .json file and transposed to standard format using pandas.

games_raw = pd.read_json("data/games.json")
games_raw = games_raw.T



Dropping Columns
For this analysis, I decided not to use unstructured text or image data. Columns containing this type of information were dropped, along with others that would not be useful for analytical purposes. See comments for further justification.

games_dropped = games_raw.drop(columns=["name", # ID variable
                                        "detailed_description", # unstructured text
                                        "about_the_game", # unstructured text
                                        "short_description", # unstructured text
                                        "reviews", # unstructured text
                                        "header_image", # image data
                                        "website", # high cardinality & sparse representation
                                        "support_url", # high cardinality & sparse representation
                                        "support_email", # high cardinality & sparse representation
                                        "windows", # zero variance
                                        "metacritic_url", # high cardinality & sparse representation
                                        "average_playtime_2weeks", # not reflective of historic data
                                        "median_playtime_2weeks", # not reflective of historic data
                                        "notes", # unstructured text
                                        "packages", # not comparable across games
                                        "developers", # high cardinality & sparse representation
                                        "publishers", # high cardinality & sparse representation
                                        "screenshots", # image data
                                        "movies", # zero variance
                                        "user_score", # extreme missingness
                                        "score_rank", # extreme missingness
                                        "discount" # not reflective of historic data
                                        ])



Missingness & Filtering Rows
This dataset does not contain any true missing values. Instead, 0 is a stand-in for missing values in numeric columns, and “” is a stand-in in string-valued columns. In most cases, this choice makes sense - “no achievements” and “zero achievements” mean the same thing - but in the case of metacritic_score, a real zero would indicate a bad score, so it was more appropriate to treat zeroes there as missing values. Furthermore, rows in which metacritic_score == 0 lack an entry in the metacritic_url column, indicating that they were never reviewed by Metacritic.
As for the remainder of the columns still included in the dataframe, I have verified that a zero truly means zero. The one remaining categorical column - estimated_owners - does not contain any placeholder values.
Since metacritic_score is my target variable, I dropped rows in which metacritic_score == 0.

# drop all rows where the target variable is null
games_dropped = games_dropped[games_dropped["metacritic_score"] != 0]



Typing Features
Due to the data being loaded from a .json, all features were initially typed as object. This had to be corrected manually.

# sort features by desired type - this must be done manually
num_features = ["required_age", 
                "price",
                "dlc_count", 
                "metacritic_score", 
                "achievements", 
                "recommendations",
                "positive",
                "negative",
                "average_playtime_forever",
                "median_playtime_forever",
                "peak_ccu"
                ]

bool_features = ["mac", "linux"]

cat_features = ["estimated_owners"]

datetime_features = ["release_date"]

list_features = ["supported_languages",
                 "full_audio_languages",
                 "categories",
                 "genres"
                ]

dict_features = ["tags"]

# type features appropriately
games_typed= games_dropped.copy()

# numerics
for f in num_features:
    games_typed[f] = games_typed[f].astype(float)

# binary columns
for f in bool_features:
    games_typed[f] = games_typed[f].astype(int)

# categories
for f in cat_features:
    games_typed[f] = pd.Categorical(games_typed[f])

# datetimes
for f in datetime_features:
    games_typed[f] = pd.to_datetime(games_typed[f])
    games_typed[str(f) + "_year"] = games_typed[f].dt.year
    games_typed[str(f) + "_month"] = games_typed[f].dt.month

# dict columns
for f in dict_features:
    # an empty list is used as a placeholder for games with no tags
    # so we can fill those in with an empty dict to be consistent with the rest of the column
    games_typed[f] = games_typed[f].apply(lambda x: {} if x == [] else x)
    f_expanded = pd.json_normalize(games_typed[f])
    # add prefix
    f_expanded = f_expanded.add_prefix(f + "_")
    # align index with original dataframe
    f_expanded.index = games_dropped.index
    # concatenate with original dataframe
    games_typed = pd.concat([games_typed, f_expanded], axis=1)
    # drop original dict column
    games_typed = games_typed.drop(columns=[f])

# fill NaNs created by empty dicts with 0s - this is appropriate since a missing tag is equivalent to a tag with a value of 0
games_typed = games_typed.fillna(0)
# (note that we had no NaNs in the original dataframe, so any NaNs in games_typed were created by the dict expansion process)



Multi-Hot Encoding
A number of columns (those included in list_columns above) contained a list of values. For instance, a value of supported_languages may be ["English", "Spanish"]. These needed to be multi-hot encoded before I could use them in my analysis.

games_encoded = games_typed.copy()
for f in list_features:
    mlb = MultiLabelBinarizer()
    transformed = mlb.fit_transform(games_typed[f])
    transformed_df = pd.DataFrame(transformed, columns=[f + "_" + str(c) for c in mlb.classes_], index=games_typed.index)
    games_encoded = pd.concat([games_encoded, transformed_df], axis=1)
    # drop original column
    games_encoded = games_encoded.drop(columns=[f])

With the data cleaning complete for now, I opted to save this cleaned dataframe as a .csv for ease of use later on.

games_encoded.to_csv("data/games_clean.csv")

I began by doing some modest tuning on my prexisting baseline Random Forest and XGBoost Models. This required loading the data from games_clean.csv and doing some minor preprocessing to prepare it to be used by my pipelines.

# load data
games = pd.read_csv("data/games_clean.csv")
games = games.drop(columns=["Unnamed: 0"]) # drop index column created by pandas when saving to csv

# fix typings
# convert datetime to unix timestamp
games["release_date"] = pd.to_datetime(games["release_date"], errors="coerce")
games["release_date"] = games["release_date"].astype("int64") // 10**9 # convert from nanoseconds to seconds
games["release_date"] = games["release_date"].astype("float64")

# convert estimated_owners to ordered categorical
games["estimated_owners"] = pd.Categorical(games["estimated_owners"],
                                           categories=["0 - 0",
                                                  "0 - 20000",
                                                  "20000 - 50000",
                                                  "50000 - 100000",
                                                  "100000 - 200000",
                                                  "200000 - 500000",
                                                  "500000 - 1000000",
                                                  "1000000 - 2000000",
                                                  "2000000 - 5000000",
                                                  "5000000 - 10000000",
                                                  "10000000 - 20000000",
                                                  "20000000 - 50000000",
                                                  "50000000 - 100000000",
                                                  "100000000 - 200000000"
                                                ], 
                                           ordered=True)

I followed the typical workflow of separating features into lists that would need to be processed in different ways according to their type.

# general feature categorization
ord_features = ["estimated_owners"]
nom_features = games.select_dtypes(include=["int32", "int64"]).drop(columns=["release_date_month", 
                                                                             "release_date_year"]).columns.tolist()

date_features = ["release_date_year", "release_date_month"]
num_features = games.select_dtypes(include=["float64"]).drop(columns=["metacritic_score"]).columns.tolist() + date_features

features = ord_features + nom_features + num_features
target = "metacritic_score"

I also split the data into training and test sets, and set up a RepeatedKFold object to be used during cross validation.

# split data 
games_train, games_test = train_test_split(
    games,
    test_size=0.2,
    random_state=4025
)

rkf = RepeatedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=3, random_state=4025)

Since both models I was planning to tune were based on decision trees, I used the same preprocessing pipeline for both of them.

# general decision tree preprocessing pipeline
dt_ord_prep = Pipeline([
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("ordinal_encoder", OrdinalEncoder())
])

dt_nom_prep = Pipeline([
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
    ("onehot_encoder", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="if_binary")),
    ("variance_threshold", VarianceThreshold(threshold=0.01))
])

dt_num_prep = Pipeline([
    ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"))
])

dt_prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("ord", dt_ord_prep, ord_features),
    ("nom", dt_nom_prep, nom_features),
    ("num", dt_num_prep, num_features)
])



My random forest tuning grid is shown below. I chose to use an exhaustive grid search since I focused on tuning only max_features.

# initial random forest pipeline & tuning grid
rf_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("preprocessor", dt_prep),
    ("model", RandomForestRegressor(random_state=4025))
])

rf_param_grid = {"model__max_features": np.linspace(350, 425, 25, dtype=int)}
                # note that this parameter grid was initially much wider
                # I narrowed it to the current range after determining it was the optimal area
                # over multiple tuning iterations

rf_grid_search = GridSearchCV(
    rf_pipe,
    rf_param_grid,
    cv=rkf,
    scoring=["neg_mean_squared_error", "r2"],
    refit="neg_mean_squared_error",
    n_jobs=-1
)

try: 
    best_rf = pickle.load(open("saved_objects/rf.pkl", "rb"))

    rf_grid_search.fit(games_train[features], games_train[target])

# initial XGB pipeline & tuning grid

    ("preprocessor", dt_prep),
    ("model", XGBRegressor())
])

    "model__max_depth": list(np.linspace(3, 10, 8, dtype=int)) + [None],
    "model__learning_rate": np.logspace(-3, 0, 10)

    xgb_pipe,
    xgb_param_grid,
    n_iter=100,
    cv=rkf,

print("XGBoost RMSE:", xgb_rmse)

While the performance metrics of my models were significantly better than the dummy regressor, I felt that they could still be improved. My dataset had a large number of features, clocking in at over 700 in total, and so I thought that using PCA or a similar method to collapse those features into a more reasonable amount might improve my performance. I had originally intended to use PCA for this, but during my implementation of it I came across sklearn’s TruncatedSVD, which was better suited to the sparse binary data that made up most of my dataset.
Implementing this method required changes to my feature lists and pipeline. To avoid any potential overlap with previously created objects, I opted to work off of a copy of the games dataset. The modified preprocessing is shown below.

games_pca = games.copy()

lang_cols = games_pca.filter(like="supported_languages_").columns.tolist()
audio_cols = games_pca.filter(like="full_audio_languages_").columns.tolist()
cat_cols = games_pca.filter(like="categories_").columns.tolist()
genre_cols = games_pca.filter(like="genres_").columns.tolist()
tag_cols = games_pca.filter(like="tags_").columns.tolist()

all_cluster_cols = lang_cols + audio_cols + cat_cols + genre_cols + tag_cols

pca_ord_features = ["estimated_owners"]
pca_nom_features = ["mac", "linux"]
pca_num_features = ["release_date",
                    "required_age",
                    "price",
                    "dlc_count",
                    "achievements",
                    "recommendations",
                    "positive",
                    "negative",
                    "average_playtime_forever",
                    "median_playtime_forever",
                    "peak_ccu",
                    "release_date_year", 
                    "release_date_month"]

pca_features = pca_ord_features + pca_nom_features + pca_num_features + all_cluster_cols
target = "metacritic_score"

pca_games_train, pca_games_test = train_test_split(
    games_pca,
    test_size=0.2,
    random_state=4025
)

To use TruncatedSVD properly, I had to specify the number of components I wanted it to create from each feature group. I did this by executing the following code for each relevant feature group, and noting which values captured 85% and 90% of variance in the group.

svd = TruncatedSVD(n_components=x, random_state=4025)

print(svd.explained_variance_ratio_.cumsum())

I also implemented functions that would allow me to easily insert pipelines with the proper parameters into my workflow.

def binary_processor(n_components):
    return Pipeline([
        ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
        ("threshold", VarianceThreshold(threshold=0.01)),
        ("svd", TruncatedSVD(n_components=n_components, random_state=4025))
    ])

def tag_processor(n_components):
    return Pipeline([
        ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("scaler", MaxAbsScaler()),
        ("svd", TruncatedSVD(n_components=n_components, random_state=4025))
    ])

I tested both 85% and 90% variance n_components with simple cross-validation.



pca_dt_prep_85 = ColumnTransformer([
    ("ord", dt_ord_prep, pca_ord_features),
    ("nom", dt_nom_prep, pca_nom_features),
    ("num", dt_num_prep, pca_num_features),
    ("lang", binary_processor(13), lang_cols),
    ("audio", binary_processor(11), audio_cols),
    ("cat", binary_processor(18), cat_cols),
    ("genre", binary_processor(6), genre_cols),
    ("tag", tag_processor(6), tag_cols)
])

pca_dt_prep_90 = ColumnTransformer([
    ("ord", dt_ord_prep, pca_ord_features),
    ("nom", dt_nom_prep, pca_nom_features),
    ("num", dt_num_prep, pca_num_features),
    ("lang", binary_processor(16), lang_cols),
    ("audio", binary_processor(14), audio_cols),
    ("cat", binary_processor(24), cat_cols),
    ("genre", binary_processor(7), genre_cols),
    ("tag", tag_processor(11), tag_cols)
])

pca_rf_85_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("preprocessor", pca_dt_prep_85),
    ("model", RandomForestRegressor(random_state=4025))
])

pca_rf_90_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("preprocessor", pca_dt_prep_90),
    ("model", RandomForestRegressor(random_state=4025))
])

pca_xgb_85_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("preprocessor", pca_dt_prep_85),
    ("model", XGBRegressor())
])

pca_xgb_90_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("preprocessor", pca_dt_prep_90),
    ("model", XGBRegressor())
])





pca_rf_85_cv_results = cross_validate(
    pca_rf_85_pipe,
    pca_games_train[pca_features],
    pca_games_train[target],
    cv=rkf,
    scoring=["neg_mean_squared_error", "r2"]
)

pca_rf_90_cv_results = cross_validate(
    pca_rf_90_pipe,
    pca_games_train[pca_features],
    pca_games_train[target],
    cv=rkf,
    scoring=["neg_mean_squared_error", "r2"]
)

pca_xgb_85_cv_results = cross_validate(
    pca_xgb_85_pipe,
    pca_games_train[pca_features],
    pca_games_train[target],
    cv=rkf,
    scoring=["neg_mean_squared_error", "r2"]
)

pca_xgb_90_cv_results = cross_validate(
    pca_xgb_90_pipe,
    pca_games_train[pca_features],
    pca_games_train[target],
    cv=rkf,
    scoring=["neg_mean_squared_error", "r2"]
)

I decided to tune the models using the 90% variance values, since models using those performed better in simple cross-validation.

# SVD Random Forest tuning
pca_rf_param_grid = {"model__max_features": np.linspace(1, 88, 25, dtype=int)}

pca_rf_gs = GridSearchCV(
    pca_rf_90_pipe,
    pca_rf_param_grid,
    cv=rkf,
    scoring=["neg_mean_squared_error", "r2"],
    refit="neg_mean_squared_error",
    n_jobs=-1
)

try: 
    pca_best_rf = pickle.load(open("saved_objects/sdv_rf.pkl", "rb"))
except FileNotFoundError:
    pca_rf_gs.fit(pca_games_train[pca_features], pca_games_train[target])

    pca_best_rf.fit(pca_games_train[pca_features], pca_games_train[target])

print("PCA Random Forest R2:", pca_rf_r2)
print("PCA Random Forest RMSE:", pca_rf_rmse)

# SVD XGBoost tuning
pca_xgb_param_grid = {
    "model__n_estimators": np.linspace(50, 1000, 20, dtype=int),
    "model__max_depth": list(np.linspace(1, 10, 8, dtype=int)) + [None],
    "model__learning_rate": np.logspace(-3, 0, 10)
}

pca_xgb_rs = RandomizedSearchCV(
    pca_xgb_90_pipe,
    pca_xgb_param_grid,
    n_iter=100,
    cv=rkf,
    scoring=["neg_mean_squared_error", "r2"],
    refit="neg_mean_squared_error",
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=4025
)

try: 
    pca_best_xgb = pickle.load(open("saved_objects/sdv_xgb.pkl", "rb"))
except FileNotFoundError:
    pca_xgb_rs.fit(pca_games_train[pca_features], pca_games_train[target])
    pca_best_xgb = pca_xgb_rs.best_estimator_
    pca_best_xgb.fit(pca_games_train[pca_features], pca_games_train[target])

pca_xgb_preds = pca_best_xgb.predict(pca_games_test[pca_features])
pca_xgb_r2 = r2_score(pca_games_test[target], pca_xgb_preds)
pca_xgb_rmse = root_mean_squared_error(pca_games_test[target], pca_xgb_preds)
print("PCA XGBoost R2:", pca_xgb_r2)
print("PCA XGBoost RMSE:", pca_xgb_rmse)

PCA Random Forest RMSE: 7.861401568703455
PCA XGBoost R2: 0.4636022578686978
PCA XGBoost RMSE: 7.523684683599748


Unfortunately, this approach did not improve my metrics - it actually worsened them a bit.
Additionally, while not shown here, I did try models on a dataset that simply did not include the columns that I attempted SVD on. These models also showed a slight decrease in performance compared to the original tuned iteration.




For what would become the final notable iteration, I decided to expand the tuning parameter grid of my original XGBoost model to cover additional parameters. This involved a return to the original dataset and feature lists. I also engineered a new feature: the ratio of positive to negative user votes.

games=games.copy()
games["positive_negative_ratio"] = games["positive"]/(games["negative"]+1)
num_features += ["positive_negative_ratio"]
features += ["positive_negative_ratio"]

# reinitialize the sets with the new feature
games_train, games_test = train_test_split(
    games,
    test_size=0.2,
    random_state=4025
)

new_xgb_param_grid = {
    "model__n_estimators": np.linspace(300, 1500, 20, dtype=int),
    "model__max_depth": [3, 4, 5, 6, 8],
    "model__learning_rate": np.logspace(-2.5, -0.5, 10),

    # 'randomness' parameters
    "model__subsample": np.linspace(0.6, 1.0, 5), # proportion of observations available to each tree
    "model__colsample_bytree": np.linspace(0.3, 1.0, 8), # proportion of columns available to each tree

    # split allowance parameters
    "model__min_child_weight": [1, 3, 5, 10], # minimum number of samples required in a leaf
    "model__gamma": [0, 0.1, 0.3, 1], # minimum reduction in loss required to split

    # regularization parameters
    "model__reg_alpha": np.logspace(-3, 1, 10), # encourages sparsity in leaves
    "model__reg_lambda": np.logspace(-2, 2, 10), # shrinks leaf weights 
}

new_xgb_rs = RandomizedSearchCV( 
    xgb_pipe,
    new_xgb_param_grid,
    n_iter=200,
    cv=rkf,
    scoring=["neg_mean_squared_error", "r2"],
    refit="neg_mean_squared_error",
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=4025
)

try: 
    new_best_xgb = pickle.load(open("saved_objects/tuned_xgb.pkl", "rb"))
except FileNotFoundError:
    new_xgb_rs.fit(games_train[features], games_train[target])
    new_best_xgb = new_xgb_rs.best_estimator_
    new_best_xgb.fit(games_train[features], games_train[target])

new_xgb_preds = new_best_xgb.predict(games_test[features])
new_xgb_r2 = r2_score(games_test[target], new_xgb_preds)
new_xgb_rmse = root_mean_squared_error(games_test[target], new_xgb_preds)
print("New XGBoost R2:", new_xgb_r2)
print("New XGBoost RMSE:", new_xgb_rmse)

New XGBoost R2: 0.5185717254641573
New XGBoost RMSE: 7.127757438729044


This extra tuning, while very expensive both in terms of time and computation, provided a modest increase to the performance of my what would become my final model. While the metrics still aren’t impressive, they have improved a reasonable amount from where I started.

I also implemented functions that would allow me to easily insert pipelines with the proper parameters into my workflow.

def binary_processor(n_components):
    return Pipeline([
        ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
        ("threshold", VarianceThreshold(threshold=0.01)),
        ("svd", TruncatedSVD(n_components=n_components, random_state=4025))
    ])

def tag_processor(n_components):
    return Pipeline([
        ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("scaler", MaxAbsScaler()),
        ("svd", TruncatedSVD(n_components=n_components, random_state=4025))
    ])
